title: Adverse Childhood Experiences
text:
In the 1980s, the physician Vincent Felitti ran a weight-loss program at Kaiser Permanente in San Diego. He was puzzled that some patients who were losing weight successfully dropped out. Talking with them, he heard surprisingly often about abuse in childhood. Weight, for some, seemed to be a kind of protection.

Together with Robert Anda of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Felitti designed a much larger study. In 1995 and 1996, adults coming to Kaiser's San Diego clinic for routine health checkups were sent a questionnaire about their childhoods, and more than 9,500 answered. It asked about seven kinds of adversity: psychological, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up with a household member who abused alcohol or drugs, was mentally ill, had been in prison, or with a mother who was treated violently.

These patients were mostly middle class, educated and insured. Even so, more than half reported at least one category of adversity, and about one in sixteen reported four or more. The more categories a person had experienced, the higher their rates of smoking, heavy drinking, drug use, depression, suicide attempts, and diseases such as heart disease, lung disease and cancer decades later.

The ACE study changed how many doctors, schools and courts think about childhood hardship and adult health.
lesson: What happens in a home echoes through a whole life. Protecting children from violence and chaos is also protecting the adults they will become.
people: Vincent Felitti, Robert Anda and colleagues
source: Felitti, V. J., Anda, R. F., Nordenberg, D., Williamson, D. F., Spitz, A. M., Edwards, V., Koss, M. P., and Marks, J. S. (1998). Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults: The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study. American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 14(4), 245-258.
caveat: The data are retrospective and correlational, and researchers warn that an individual's ACE score cannot predict that person's future.
